*Apply-the-tool track · Job C.*

This job hunts the one kind of dependence that Pearson correlation **structurally
cannot see**: the rate at which two stocks crash *together*.  We climb the same
ladder — a toy whose answer is beyond dispute, a stylized bank pair where we can
count the co-crash by hand, then the real basket — but the **method** stays fixed
throughout: a single co-crash measure, introduced once and reused unchanged as the
data grows up. ("Co-crash" just means both names have a very bad day at the same
time.)

**What you will produce:** a tail-risk report ranking the real pairs that crash
together far more often than chance would predict — the diversification illusions a
trading desk would act on.

---

## 🧪 Rung 1 · Toy — Known Answer

Start where the truth is not in doubt, and recall *why* a single correlation number
is the wrong tool for tail risk.  `datasets.nonlinear_dependence()` draws
$y = x^2 + \text{noise}$ on a symmetric range: **$y$ is (almost) fixed once you know
$x$** — about as much dependence as you can have — yet the relationship is symmetric,
so *Pearson must read $\approx 0$*.  Pearson lies.  The lesson for this job: a single
number that averages over *all* values of $X$ can be blind to a dependence that only
lives in one *region* of the data.  Tail risk is exactly such a region — the worst
days — so an averaged-over-everything correlation will miss it.

```{python}
x_toy: Float[Array, "n"]
y_toy: Float[Array, "n"]
x_toy, y_toy = datasets.nonlinear_dependence(n=1000, noise=0.05, seed=0)   # y = x² + ε

pear = pearsonr(x_toy, y_toy)[0]      # ρ(x,y)   — linear, averaged over all x
spear = spearmanr(x_toy, y_toy)[0]    # ρ_s(x,y) — monotone, also averaged over all x

print(f"x: {x_toy.shape}    y = x² + noise   (y is ~determined by x)")
print(f"Pearson  = {pear:+.3f}   (linear — reads almost nothing)")
print(f"Spearman = {spear:+.3f}   (monotone — also blind to the symmetry)")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-toy-pearson-lies
#| fig-cap: "Pearson lies. y = x² + noise is an almost-deterministic dependence, yet Pearson ≈ 0 because the up-arm and down-arm cancel in the average. Conditioning on a *region* of x (the left arm, shaded) reveals a strong local relationship the unconditional number erased. Tail risk lives in exactly such a region — the worst days — which is why this job conditions instead of averaging."
left: Float[Array, "n"] = x_toy < 0                  # condition on a region of x (left arm)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 5.0))
ax.scatter(x_toy[~left], y_toy[~left], s=12, c="0.78", alpha=0.5, edgecolors="none",
           label="right arm (x ≥ 0)")
ax.scatter(x_toy[left], y_toy[left], s=14, c=WARM, alpha=0.8, edgecolors="none",
           label="left arm (x < 0) — strongly downward")
ax.axvline(0, color=INK, lw=0.8, ls="--")
ax.set_xlabel("x"); ax.set_ylabel("y = x² + noise")
ax.set_title(f"Pearson over all x = {pear:+.2f}, yet each arm is steep",
             fontsize=11.5)
ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="upper center"); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The known answer holds: the dependence is real and strong, but every averaged-over-everything
correlation reads $\approx 0$ because it cancels a region that bends one way against a
region that bends the other.  **The fix is to zoom in on a single region**
instead of averaging over all of $X$ — and the region a portfolio fears is the tail,
its worst days.  That is the move the next rung turns into the co-crash measure.

---

## 🎭 Rung 2 · Toy-Real — A Stylized Market

$y = x^2$ never happens in markets.  What *does* happen is **joint crashes**: two banks
that drift together on calm days and plunge together on the bad ones.
`datasets.two_banks()` is a stylized version of that — a shared driver plus a known
~10% set of days where both names crater (the `crash_mask`).  Here the answer is
again known: we built the crash days ourselves, so we can count the co-crash off the
mask by hand *and* check our estimate against that ground truth.

**The method — zoom in on the tail.**  Replace "average over all $X$" with
"look only at $X$'s worst days."  The co-crash fraction is a conditional
probability — the chance of one event *given* that another has already happened:

$$
\text{co-crash}(X, Y) \;=\; P\bigl(Y \le Q_q(Y) \,\big|\, X \le Q_q(X)\bigr)
\qquad q = 0.10,
$$

the chance that $Y$ is in *its* worst 10% of days, given that $X$ is in *its* worst
10% of days.  A pair that moves **independently** scores $\approx q = 10\%$ — that is
the baseline you compare against; a pair that crashes together scores far higher.
Spelled out, with the quadrant masks made visible:

```{python}
def cocrash_by_hand(x: Float[Array, "n"], y: Float[Array, "n"], q: float = 0.10) -> float:
    """The co-crash measure, axes spelled out — P(Y in worst-q | X in worst-q).

    qˣ = Q_q(x),  qʸ = Q_q(y)               [crash lines, return units]
    co-crash = |{ xₜ ≤ qˣ  AND  yₜ ≤ qʸ }| / |{ xₜ ≤ qˣ }|
    """
    qˣ, qʸ = np.quantile(x, q), np.quantile(y, q)   # qˣ = Q_q(x), qʸ = Q_q(y)   [return units]
    x_crash: Float[Array, "n"] = x <= qˣ            # condition: X in its worst q
    joint:   Float[Array, "n"] = einx.logical_and("n, n -> n", x_crash, y <= qʸ)   # xₜ≤qˣ ∧ yₜ≤qʸ
    return float(joint.sum() / x_crash.sum())       # P(Y crashes | X crashes)


a: Float[Array, "n"]
b: Float[Array, "n"]
a, b, crash = datasets.two_banks(n=1500, seed=0)
print(f"{int(crash.sum())} built-in crash days of {crash.size}  ({crash.mean():.0%})\n")

INDEP_BASELINE = 0.10                              # an independent pair scores ≈ q
cc_hand = cocrash_by_hand(a, b)                    # our spelled-out version
cc_lib  = cocrash_fraction(a, b, q=0.10)           # the library measure — must agree
print(f"co-crash (by hand)   = {cc_hand:.1%}")
print(f"co-crash (library)   = {cc_lib:.1%}   ← same number, reused everywhere above")
print(f"independence baseline= {INDEP_BASELINE:.1%}")
print(f"lift over baseline   = {cc_lib / INDEP_BASELINE:.1f}×")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-twobanks-cocrash
#| fig-cap: "The stylized bank pair, with the co-crash quadrant shaded. The condition is the 10% of days bank A falls hardest (left band); the co-crash fraction is the share of those days on which B also breaks its crash line (red) versus shrugs it off (blue). The built-in crash days (the shared shock) pile into the lower-left corner, lifting co-crash far above the 10% independence baseline — exactly the tail an unconditional Pearson under-reads."
qᵃ, qᵇ = np.quantile(a, 0.10), np.quantile(b, 0.10)   # qᵃ = Q₀.₁₀(a), qᵇ = Q₀.₁₀(b)   [return units]
band: Float[Array, "n"] = a <= qᵃ                      # condition: A in its worst 10%
co:   Float[Array, "n"] = band & (b <= qᵇ)             # aₜ≤qᵃ ∧ bₜ≤qᵇ → a co-crash
hold: Float[Array, "n"] = band & (b > qᵇ)              # aₜ≤qᵃ ∧ bₜ>qᵇ → B held up

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 5.2))
ax.axvspan(a.min(), qᵃ, color=CRASH, alpha=0.06)
ax.axhline(qᵇ, color=INK, lw=0.8, ls=":")
ax.scatter(a[~band], b[~band], s=8, c="0.78", alpha=0.3, edgecolors="none")
ax.scatter(a[hold], b[hold], s=26, c=COOL, alpha=0.8, edgecolors="none",
           label=f"A crashes, B holds  ({int(hold.sum())})")
ax.scatter(a[co], b[co], s=30, c=CRASH, alpha=0.9, edgecolors="none",
           label=f"both crash — a co-crash  ({int(co.sum())})")
ax.text(qᵃ, ax.get_ylim()[1], "  condition: A in its worst 10%",
        color=CRASH, fontsize=9, va="top", ha="left")
ax.set_xlabel("bank A return"); ax.set_ylabel("bank B return")
ax.set_title(f"Of A's {int(band.sum())} worst days, B also craters on "
             f"{int(co.sum())}  →  co-crash {cc_lib:.0%}", fontsize=11.5)
ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="upper left"); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

There are two things to take away here.  First, the measure is **correct**: the
by-hand quadrant count and `cocrash_fraction` return the same number, and it sits far
above the 10% baseline — the co-crash is real, because we built it in.  Second, this
is *exactly* the tail that a correlation number under-reports: Pearson averages the
calm cloud and the crash corner together, while the co-crash measure keeps only the
corner.  We now carry this same measure, unchanged, onto the real book of stocks.

---

## 📈 Rung 3 · Real — The Full Basket

**What we are looking for on real data:** pairs of stocks that look safely
unrelated in calm times yet fall together when markets break.  The co-crash number
tells us, for each pair, how often the second name has one of its worst days on the
same day the first name does — high means dangerous, near 10% means genuinely
independent.

**Receiving Tool 1's handoff.**  [Tool 1's
watchlist](lab-tool1-ladder.qmd) ranked real pairs by their `Pearson − Spearman`
gap — a cheap, quick clue that some cross-sector pairs only move together on extreme
days.  The flagged names were the **diversification illusions**: utilities and
energy against the rest (e.g. `CVX/DUK`, `XOM/DUK`, `GS/DUK`).  Tool 1 could only
*flag* them; this job runs the co-crash test that confirms the tail coupling
rigorously — something no averaged-over-everything measure on that road can do.

We **reload** the already-prepared returns — there is no cleaning here; the
prices → log-returns pipeline and the crash-mask setting live in the data primer —
display a corner of the table, and run the *same* `cocrash_fraction` from Rung 2.

```{python}
R = datasets.load_returns()                       # prepared 14-name daily panel
META = datasets.load_basket_meta()
label  = dict(zip(META["ticker"], META["label"]))
sector = dict(zip(META["ticker"], META["sector"]))
tickers = list(R.columns)
print(f"{len(R)} trading days × {len(tickers)} stocks   "
      f"({R.index.min().date()} → {R.index.max().date()})")
R[["JPM", "BAC", "GS", "XOM", "CVX", "DUK"]].iloc[:3].round(4)
```

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Where This Data Comes From
The panel, the crash-day mask, and the co-crash statistic this job rides on are laid
bare in the data primer —
[Crashes & Drawdowns](../../data/03-crashes-and-drawdowns.qmd) defines the
percentile crash dial, and [Co-Movement &
Co-Crashes](../../data/04-co-movement-and-co-crashes.qmd) builds the co-crash

masks or the sectors.

First, settle Tool 1's handoff directly: run the conditional co-crash test on those
exact flagged pairs, against the independence baseline.

```{python}
WATCHLIST = [("CVX", "DUK"), ("XOM", "DUK"), ("GS", "DUK")]   # Tool 1's flagged pairs

print("Tool 1's diversification-illusion pairs, under the conditional test:\n")
print(f"{'pair':<10s}{'Pearson':>9s}{'co-crash':>10s}{'lift':>7s}  sectors")
print("-" * 50)
for u, v in WATCHLIST:
    xu: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R[u].values
    xv: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R[v].values

    pe = pearsonr(xu, xv)[0]                        # ρ(u,v) — what Tool 1 could see
    cc = cocrash_fraction(xu, xv, q=0.10)           # P(v crash | u crash) — conditional tail test
    lift = cc / INDEP_BASELINE                      # lift = co-crash / q

    print(f"{u + '/' + v:<10s}{pe:>+9.3f}{cc:>9.0%}{lift:>6.1f}×"
          f"  {sector[u]}/{sector[v]}")
```

The handoff is confirmed: these cross-sector pairs have only a **modest Pearson
correlation** (they look diversified in calm times) yet crash together several times
more often than the 10% baseline — the tail coupling Tool 1 could flag but not
measure.  Now the full-basket sweep: run the same measure on every pair and assemble
the co-crash matrix.

```{python}
import itertools

rows = []
for u, v in itertools.combinations(tickers, 2):
    xu: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R[u].values
    xv: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R[v].values

    cc = cocrash_fraction(xu, xv, q=0.10)          # P(v crash | u crash) — the Rung-2 measure, unchanged
    rows.append(dict(pair=f"{u}/{v}", u=u, v=v,
                     same_sector=(sector[u] == sector[v]),
                     pearson=pearsonr(xu, xv)[0],  # ρ(u,v)
                     cocrash=cc,
                     lift=cc / INDEP_BASELINE))     # lift = co-crash / q
rows.sort(key=lambda r: r["cocrash"], reverse=True)
print(f"{len(rows)} pairs measured.  strongest co-crashes:\n")
print(f"{'pair':<10s}{'Pearson':>9s}{'co-crash':>10s}{'lift':>7s}  sector")
print("-" * 48)
for r in rows[:8]:
    print(f"{r['pair']:<10s}{r['pearson']:>+9.3f}{r['cocrash']:>9.0%}"
          f"{r['lift']:>6.1f}×  {'same' if r['same_sector'] else 'cross'}")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-cocrash-matrix-compute
order = sorted(tickers, key=lambda t: (sector[t], t))   # group columns by sector
n = len(order)

CC: Float[Array, "n_assets n_assets"] = np.eye(n)       # CC[i,j] = P(i crash | j crash); diag = 1
for i, u in enumerate(order):
    for j, v in enumerate(order):
        if i != j:
            xu: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R[u].values
            xv: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R[v].values
            CC[i, j] = cocrash_fraction(xv, xu, q=0.10)  # P(u crash | v crash) — condition on column v

secs = [sector[t] for t in order]                       # sector label per column
bounds = [i for i in range(1, n) if secs[i] != secs[i - 1]]   # indices where the sector changes
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-cocrash-matrix
#| fig-cap: "The full-basket co-crash matrix, ordered by sector. Each cell is P(row crashes | column crashes) at the 10% tail; the diagonal is 1 by construction. The bank block (top-left) glows — when one bank has a worst-decile day, the others crater with it ~65–70% of the time — but the off-diagonal cross-sector cells are far from the 10% baseline too, the systemic coupling that surfaces only in the tail. This is the conditional structure Pearson averages away."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.4, 6.4))
im = ax.imshow(CC, cmap="inferno", vmin=0.10, vmax=1.0)
ax.set_xticks(range(n)); ax.set_xticklabels(order, rotation=90, fontsize=8)
ax.set_yticks(range(n)); ax.set_yticklabels(order, fontsize=8)
for b in bounds:                                        # draw the sector dividers
    ax.axhline(b - 0.5, color="white", lw=1.0); ax.axvline(b - 0.5, color="white", lw=1.0)
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.046, label="co-crash  P(row | column)")
ax.set_title("Co-crash matrix — coupling that only shows in the tail", fontsize=12)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Read the matrix: the bank block is the obvious hot square, but the cross-sector cells
away from the diagonal sit well above the 10% floor too — the market-wide drag that
makes a "diversified" book fall as one.  The ranking below turns this into the
deliverable.

## 💰 Rung 4 · Application — The Tail-Risk Flag

The deliverable is a **tail-risk report**, and it has two lists.  The raw co-crash
ranking is topped by the obvious same-sector pairs (the banks crash together, the
energy majors crash together — everyone already knows that), so the report ranks the
two groups *separately*: a within-sector list (the already-known coupling, useful for
position sizing) and a **cross-sector** list — the diversification illusions.  For
that second group, a correlation-based risk model sets aside too little capital,
because Pearson sees only the calm-time relationship and misses the joint crash.
That second list is what Tool 1 handed off and what a trading desk would actually act
on.

```{python}
#| label: fig-tailrisk-flag
#| fig-cap: "The tail-risk flag, split into the two queues a desk reads differently. Within-sector pairs (blue, bottom) are the already-known coupling — the bank and energy blocks crash as one. The cross-sector pairs (red, top) are the report's payload: the diversification illusions, loosely correlated in calm times yet dragged together in 2008 and 2020, far above the 10% independence baseline (dashed). These are the pairs Tool 1 flagged and a covariance-based risk model under-reserves."
within = [r for r in rows if r["same_sector"]][:8]      # known coupling — for sizing
cross  = [r for r in rows if not r["same_sector"]][:8]  # the diversification illusions

for title, queue in [("within-sector  (known coupling)", within),
                     ("cross-sector  (diversification illusions → act on these)", cross)]:
    print(f"\n{title}\n{'pair':<10s}{'Pearson':>9s}{'co-crash':>10s}{'lift':>7s}")
    print("-" * 36)
    for r in queue:
        print(f"{r['pair']:<10s}{r['pearson']:>+9.3f}{r['cocrash']:>9.0%}{r['lift']:>6.1f}×")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.8, 4.6))
queue = within[::-1] + cross[::-1]                      # barh: within fills the bottom, cross the top
colors = [COOL] * len(within) + [CRASH] * len(cross)
ax.barh([r["pair"] for r in queue], [100 * r["cocrash"] for r in queue], color=colors)
ax.axvline(100 * INDEP_BASELINE, color=INK, lw=1.2, ls="--",
           label="independence baseline (10%)")
ax.axhline(len(within) - 0.5, color=INK, lw=0.8)        # divider between the two queues
ax.text(0.99, len(within) - 0.5, "within-sector ", transform=ax.get_yaxis_transform(),
        ha="right", va="top", fontsize=9, color=COOL, fontweight="bold")
ax.text(0.99, len(within) + len(cross) - 0.5, "cross-sector ", transform=ax.get_yaxis_transform(),
        ha="right", va="top", fontsize=9, color=CRASH, fontweight="bold")
ax.set_xlabel("co-crash  (% of one name's worst days the other also crashes)")
ax.set_title("Tail-risk flag — two queues a desk reads differently", fontsize=12)
ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="lower right")
despine(ax); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Read the cross-sector list as the triage queue: these are the pairs whose joint
crashes a covariance matrix most badly understates, by counting them as a
diversification benefit that is not really there.  They look diversified to Pearson
and are not, in the only situation that matters — the bad days — and they crash
together two to three times more often than the baseline despite modest correlation,
exactly the illusion Tool 1 flagged and this test confirms.

---

## How Deep Is the Illusion? Sweep the Tail

The co-crash setting `q` controls how bad a day has to be to count as a "crash" — a
smaller `q` means a deeper, rarer loss.  The diversification illusion is not fixed: it
gets **worse** the further into the tail you look.  Sweep `q` for the flagged
cross-sector pairs:

```{python}
print(f"{'pair':<10s}{'q=20%':>8s}{'q=10%':>8s}{'q=5%':>8s}   (co-crash lift over baseline)")
for pair in ["CVX/DUK", "XOM/DUK", "GS/DUK"]:
    a, b = pair.split("/")
    x: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R[a].to_numpy()
    y: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R[b].to_numpy()

    lift = [cocrash_fraction(x, y, q=q) / q for q in (0.20, 0.10, 0.05)]   # lift = P(y crash|x crash) / q
    print(f"{pair:<10s}{lift[0]:>7.1f}x{lift[1]:>7.1f}x{lift[2]:>7.1f}x")
```

The pattern is the warning.  At a mild 20% threshold these pairs crash together under
twice as often as the baseline — easy to wave away — but zoom in on the *worst 5%* of
days and that multiple roughly triples, to about 6×.  The tail dependence a covariance
matrix misses is worst exactly where it hurts most: in the deepest losses.  This is the
flag a desk acts on, and the reason the [uncertainty](../../uncertainty/index.qmd)
chapter refuses to model the joint tail with a Gaussian, and the
[gaussianization](../../gaussianization/index.qmd) chapter learns the true joint shape
instead.
